correctness.rationale: The ten nonmerged unordered pairs form an exact deterministic two-letter transition graph with a merge sink. Successive predecessor levels compute the shortest successful path, and no successful shortest path repeats a pair, giving a bound of ten. Independent forward-level and reverse-BFS C++17 programs separately enumerate all \(5^{10}\) ordered letter maps and agree on all ten frequencies, the nonsynchronizing total, and the extremal count. Exhaustive symmetry-orbit comparison certifies one radius-ten class. These are checked computations backed by fully replayable source, not extrapolation from samples.

originality.rationale: The full distribution of maximum prescribed-pair merge times across binary five-state automata and the exhaustive uniqueness of its extremal orbit are not supplied by the examined primary texts: the 2026 survey records the prescribed-pair bound and Černý tightness, while the 2016 census enumerates global reset thresholds. Two automata with reset threshold four and different prescribed-pair radii demonstrate that earlier reset-length data cannot logically determine this statistic. Actual research-record searches returned different synchronization invariants, including triple rendezvous and unconstrained merging of a fixed state. Historical priority cannot be guaranteed against inaccessible or unindexed equivalent tables.
residual_risks: An earlier, unindexed complete table of pair-synchronization radii for binary five-state automata may exist.
The findings are not independently externally audited, and the finite computer proof depends on correctly compiling and replaying the included source code.

value.rationale: Synchronizing every prescribed state pair is the exact pair-graph condition underlying deterministic-automaton synchronization algorithms. The complete distribution quantifies the hardest pair-merging task for the natural full five-state binary ensemble, supplies an exact conditional mean, and classifies every sharp case under the natural symmetry group. It is a complete and interpretable finite benchmark, not a routine restatement of the already known universal upper bound.
